summary: Current IS-IS flooding rates are much slower than modern networks can support, and larger deployments need faster flooding to meet convergence goals. This experimental document discusses the need and the issues, describes example approaches, and defines related protocol extensions.

eli5.summary: Routers pass news to each other, but they do it slowly, like passing notes one at a time. This experiment speeds up passing the notes without overwhelming anyone.

questions: how to speed up is-is lsp flooding
subtitle: Speeding up router-to-router topology updates for larger networks

tldr.problem: Large networks need routers to share topology updates at rates much faster than the 33-millisecond intervals defined in the original IS-IS specification, which can cause convergence delays of a minute or more when a node with thousands of neighbors fails.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines new TLV fields to let neighboring routers advertise their ability to send and receive LSPs at faster rates, introduces flow and congestion control algorithms similar to TCP, and recommends faster acknowledgment of received updates.
tldr.outcome: Networks can now flood topology updates 100 times faster or more, reducing convergence time to seconds instead of minutes, which is essential for modern large-scale deployments.

facts.label: Convergence time
facts.value: Reduced from 60+ seconds to 5-10 seconds on large failures

today: RFC 9681 is an Experimental specification that has not been adopted into the Internet Standards Track. However, vendors are testing and implementing the mechanisms to verify whether faster flooding improves convergence in large deployments without destabilizing networks.

sections.title: The Flooding Bottleneck
sections.content:
IS-IS is a routing protocol that works by flooding, where each router tells all its neighbors about the network topology, and they pass it along. The original IS-IS spec from 1992 set very conservative timing rules: routers had to wait at least 33 milliseconds between sending Link State PDUs (LSPs), and could only send 10 LSPs per second. This was fine when networks were small and CPUs were slow.

But today, large networks have routers with thousands of neighbors. When such a router fails, it generates 1000 or more LSP updates. At 33 LSPs per second, it takes 30 seconds just to send those updates to one neighbor, and the rest of the network must then receive and process them. The total convergence time can stretch to a minute or more, during which traffic can be misrouted.
sections.eli5: When a big router fails, it sends lots of messages to its neighbors. Old rules make them wait 33 milliseconds between each message, so it takes forever to hear the news.

sections.title: Faster Flooding Parameters
sections.content:
This RFC defines a new TLV called the Flooding Parameters TLV that routers send in IS-IS Hellos and PSNPs to advertise what rates they can sustain. The key sub-TLVs are:

LSP Burst Size: the number of LSPs a router can receive back to back without waiting. Typically 5 to 20.

LSP Transmission Interval: the minimum gap (in microseconds) between LSPs after a burst ends. This replaces the rigid 33-millisecond rule and can be as low as 1 millisecond on modern hardware.

LSPs per PSNP: when this many unacknowledged LSPs arrive, send an immediate acknowledgment instead of waiting for a timer. A value of 15 is recommended.

Receive Window: the maximum number of unacknowledged LSPs a router will buffer, similar to TCP's window size. Values of 50 to 100 are typical.
sections.eli5: Routers now tell each other: I can accept 20 messages at once, then I need at least 1 millisecond between the next ones, and I'll acknowledge every 15 messages. Each router respects what the other one says it can handle.

sections.title: Flow and Congestion Control
sections.content:
The RFC introduces two sender-side algorithms for managing traffic:

Flow Control uses a receive window, like TCP. The sender tracks how many LSPs the receiver has acknowledged and does not send more LSPs than the window allows. When the receiver acknowledges LSPs, the window opens up again, permitting more sending.

Congestion Control starts with a congestion window equal to the LSP Burst Size plus one. As LSPs are acknowledged, the window grows slowly (congestion avoidance phase), allowing higher rates. If losses are detected—either by a timeout or by receiving acknowledgments out of order—the window shrinks back down (congestion signal). A fast recovery phase can speed recovery after loss.

The algorithms also recommend pacing: spreading LSP transmissions evenly over time rather than sending them in bursts, using a leaky bucket algorithm or similar technique.
sections.eli5: The sender keeps track of how much the receiver has accepted and stops before flooding it. If nothing gets lost, the sender slowly tries faster rates. If something is lost, it backs off.

sections.title: Receiver Improvements
sections.content:
The RFC recommends that receivers also optimize their side of the link. Receivers should send PSNPs (Partial Sequence Number PDUs, which acknowledge received LSPs) much faster than the original 2-second interval. A 200-millisecond interval is more typical today.

Additionally, when unacknowledged LSPs reach the LSPs-per-PSNP threshold, the receiver should send a PSNP immediately without waiting for the timer. This closes the feedback loop faster, allowing the sender to detect that LSPs are being received and to continue transmitting.

On the receiver side, implementations should prioritize incoming IS-IS packets: Hellos first (to keep the adjacency alive), then SNPs, then LSPs. This ensures that a burst of LSPs does not trigger an adjacency timeout that would require even more LSPs to be sent.
sections.eli5: The receiver sends quick acknowledgments and gives priority to hello messages so it does not accidentally forget about a neighbor in the middle of a flood.

sections.title: Deployment Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC is marked Experimental, inviting implementations to test the approach. Different implementations and hardware may benefit from different parameter values. The document suggests some baseline recommendations based on hardware available at the time of publication: a burst size of 10 (conservative) to 20, a transmission interval of 1 to 33 milliseconds (33 is conservative), and a receive window of 30 to 200 (with 60 as a typical value).

On broadcast LAN interfaces (like Ethernet shared by many routers), the solution is more complex because each router receives LSPs from multiple senders and must apply the most conservative advertised parameters. The RFC notes that LAN behavior was out of scope and focuses on point-to-point links, which are preferred for better performance.

These extensions are optional and backward compatible: routers that do not support them continue to use the old slow rates, but mixed deployments can work as long as each side respects the capabilities advertised by the other.
sections.eli5: The faster rates are optional and vary by router model. On a shared network, every router has to use the slowest router's limits. Routers that do not support the faster rates still work, just slowly.
